specStatements.text: When certain insulating materials are rubbed against each other they become electrically charged. Negatively charged electrons are rubbed off one material and on to the other. The material that gains electrons becomes negatively charged. The material that loses electrons is left with an equal positive charge.

When two electrically charged objects are brought close together they exert a force on each other. Two objects that carry the same type of charge repel. Two objects that carry different types of charge attract. Attraction and repulsion between two charged objects are examples of non-contact force.
• describe the production of static electricity, and sparking, by rubbing surfaces
• describe evidence that charged objects exert forces of attraction or repulsion on one another when not in contact
• explain how the transfer of electrons between objects can explain the phenomena of static electricity.
A charged object creates an electric field around itself. The electric field is strongest close to the charged object. The further away from the charged object, the weaker the field.
A second charged object placed in the field experiences a force. The force gets stronger as the distance between the objects decreases.
• draw the electric field pattern for an isolated charged sphere
• explain the concept of an electric field
• explain how the concept of an electric field helps to explain the non-contact force between charged objects as well as other electrostatic phenomena such as sparking.

scopeNotes.statement: • draw the electric field pattern for an isolated charged sphere
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Only the isolated charged sphere is taught and tested: straight radial lines spreading out in all directions, evenly spaced around the sphere, drawn closer together near the surface, with arrows away from a positive sphere and towards a negative one. No pattern for a pair of charges, for parallel plates, or for any combination of fields is drawn or asked for, because the specification names only the isolated sphere.

scopeNotes.statement: When certain insulating materials are rubbed against each other they become electrically charged.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Charging by rubbing is applied only to insulating materials, as the specification states, and never presented as something any material will do. Conductors appear only to honour the specification's own word 'insulating' - to explain why charge does not stay on a metal rod held in the hand. No triboelectric series is taught, and no claim is made about which particular material gains and which loses electrons in an unfamiliar pair; questions always state which object ends up negatively charged.

scopeNotes.statement: A second charged object placed in the field experiences a force. The force gets stronger as the distance between the objects decreases.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The relationship between force and distance is kept qualitative, exactly as the specification words it: closer means stronger. No inverse-square relationship, no Coulomb's law, no equation for field strength and no numerical field or force calculation is introduced, because the specification supplies no such equation for this section.

concepts.definition: Electric charge that has built up on an object and stays where it is, rather than flowing as a current. It is produced when certain insulating materials are rubbed against each other.
When certain insulating materials are rubbed against each other they become electrically charged: negatively charged electrons are rubbed off one material and on to the other.
The movement of electrons from one object to another. Only electrons move when objects are rubbed; the positively charged nuclei stay fixed in place in the material.
An object that has gained electrons. The material that gains electrons in rubbing becomes negatively charged.
An object that has lost electrons. The material that loses electrons is left with a positive charge, because it now has more positive charge in its nuclei than negative charge in its electrons.
The material that loses electrons is left with a charge equal in size to the negative charge on the material that gains them, because every electron gained by one is an electron lost by the other.
A material that charge cannot flow through. Charge produced by rubbing stays on the surface of an insulator instead of flowing away, which is why static charge can build up on it.
Two objects that carry the same type of charge repel: two negatively charged objects push each other apart, and so do two positively charged objects.
Two objects that carry different types of charge attract: a positively charged object and a negatively charged object pull each other together.
A force that acts between two objects that are not touching. Attraction and repulsion between two charged objects are examples of non-contact force.

As charge builds up on an object by rubbing, the potential difference between it and a nearby earthed object grows. When it is large enough, charge moves across the gap through the air, and this sudden movement of charge is seen and heard as a spark.

concepts.term: Ionisation of the air in a spark
concepts.definition: When the electric field in the gap becomes strong enough, it pulls electrons off atoms in the air. The air then contains charged particles that are free to move, so it can conduct, and charge flows across the gap as a spark.
The region around a charged object in which another charged object experiences a force. A charged object creates an electric field around itself.
The electric field is strongest close to the charged object, and the further away from the charged object, the weaker the field.

concepts.term: Electric field pattern for an isolated charged sphere
concepts.definition: Straight lines drawn from the surface of the sphere, spreading out evenly in all directions. The arrows point away from a positively charged sphere and towards a negatively charged sphere. The lines are closest together near the surface, where the field is strongest, and spread further apart with distance, where the field is weaker.

concepts.term: Force on a second charged object
concepts.definition: A second charged object placed in the field of a charged object experiences a force. The force gets stronger as the distance between the objects decreases.

concepts.term: Field explanation of a non-contact force
concepts.definition: Each charged object creates a field around itself, and the other object sits inside that field. The force acts on each object because of the field at its own position, so the objects do not need to touch for a force to act.

concepts.term: Suspended rod test (evidence for electrostatic forces)
concepts.definition: A charged rod is hung on a thread so that it can turn freely. A second charged rod brought near it, without touching, makes it turn away if the two carry the same type of charge and turn towards if they carry different types. This is evidence that charged objects exert forces on one another when not in contact.

misconceptions.question: Does rubbing two materials together make new electric charge?
misconceptions.correct: No. Rubbing transfers electrons that were already there from one material to the other. No charge is made or destroyed.
misconceptions.misconception: Rubbing creates charge, in the same way that rubbing your hands creates heat.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students meet friction first as a way of producing heat, and 'produce static electricity' sounds like producing something new. Nothing visible moves during rubbing, so transfer is easy to miss.
misconceptions.correction: Rubbing only moves electrons about. Count them: every electron the cloth loses is an electron the rod gains, so the two charges appear together and are equal in size. If charge were being created, one object could end up charged on its own, which never happens.

misconceptions.question: When an object becomes positively charged by rubbing, have protons moved on to it?
misconceptions.correct: No. It became positive by losing electrons. Only electrons are transferred; the protons in the nuclei do not move.
misconceptions.misconception: Positive charge is rubbed on to one object and negative charge on to the other, so protons move one way and electrons the other.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Symmetry is seductive: if one object ends up negative and the other positive, students assume both types of charge must have travelled. The idea that a positive charge appears through the loss of something negative is counter-intuitive.
misconceptions.correction: Protons are locked inside nuclei in the structure of the material and cannot be rubbed off. Electrons are on the outside of atoms and can. Losing negative charge leaves an object positive - like taking coins out of a till leaves it short.

misconceptions.question: After rubbing, is the positive charge on one material the same size as the negative charge on the other?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The material that loses electrons is left with a charge equal in size to the negative charge gained by the other material.
misconceptions.misconception: One material ends up more strongly charged than the other, because it was rubbed harder or holds charge better.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Only one of the two objects is usually tested in class - the rod - so the cloth is forgotten. Students also confuse how well a material holds charge with how much charge appeared.
misconceptions.correction: Track the electrons. Each electron that leaves the cloth arrives on the rod, so the shortfall on one exactly matches the surplus on the other. Rubbing harder transfers more electrons, but it changes both charges together, and they stay equal in size and opposite in type.

misconceptions.question: Can a metal rod held in your hand be charged by rubbing it with a cloth?
misconceptions.correct: No. Electrons transferred to or from the metal flow through the metal and through your body to earth, so no charge builds up on the rod.
misconceptions.misconception: Any object can be given a static charge by rubbing it hard enough; metals just need more rubbing.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The rule is remembered as 'rubbing charges things' rather than as the specification's 'certain insulating materials'. The word insulating is treated as a detail rather than as the reason the effect works.
misconceptions.correction: Static charge stays only where it cannot flow away. On an insulator such as polythene or acetate, charge is stuck on the surface. A metal conducts, so any charge given to it runs away through your hand. Rest the same metal on an insulating stand and charge can then stay on it.

misconceptions.question: Do two objects carrying the same type of charge attract each other?
misconceptions.correct: No. Two objects that carry the same type of charge repel. Two objects that carry different types of charge attract.
misconceptions.misconception: Charged things attract other charged things, and two objects with the same charge attract most of all because they are alike.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The first demonstration most students see is a rubbed rod picking up small pieces of paper, so 'charged means sticky' is learned before the rule about types of charge. Everyday sayings about like things going together do the rest.
misconceptions.correction: Learn the pair together and test it: two rods rubbed the same way carry the same type of charge and swing apart; a polythene rod and an acetate rod carry different types and swing together. Repulsion between two charged objects is the reliable test, because only like charges repel.

misconceptions.question: Do two charged objects have to touch before a force acts between them?
misconceptions.correct: No. When two electrically charged objects are brought close together they exert a force on each other without touching. These are examples of non-contact force.
misconceptions.misconception: A push or a pull needs contact, so the objects only affect each other at the moment they touch.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Every force a student has felt directly - pushing, pulling, friction - involves contact, so a force across a gap feels like it needs an explanation before it can be believed.
misconceptions.correction: Watch a suspended charged rod: it starts to turn while the second rod is still centimetres away, and it turns further as the gap closes. The force is already acting across the gap, which is what non-contact force means.

misconceptions.question: Is a rubbed plastic rod magnetic?
misconceptions.correct: No. The rod carries electric charge. It attracts and repels other charged objects, which is a different effect from magnetism.
misconceptions.misconception: Rubbing a rod magnetises it, which is why it can pull and push things without touching them.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Magnetism is the non-contact force students meet first, and it is the only one many of them have handled. Both give attraction and repulsion across a gap, so the two effects get filed together.
misconceptions.correction: Test it. A charged polythene rod will not pick up steel paper clips or pins, and a magnet will not repel a charged acetate rod. Electrostatic forces act between charges; magnetic forces do not.

misconceptions.question: Do electric field lines show the path a charged object would travel?
misconceptions.correct: No. The lines are a way of showing where the field acts, which way the force acts, and how strong the field is. They are not tracks.
misconceptions.misconception: The lines are the routes a charge has to follow, like rails or wires running out from the object.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Lines with arrows on them look like journeys, and students have already met arrowed lines in ray diagrams, where they really do show a path.
misconceptions.correction: Read a field line as an instruction about force, not about travel: at any point on the line, the force on a positive charge points along the arrow. Where a charged object actually moves depends on that force and on any other forces on it.

misconceptions.question: What shape are the field lines around an isolated charged sphere?
misconceptions.correct: Straight lines that spread out from the sphere in all directions, evenly spaced around it.
misconceptions.misconception: The lines are circles drawn round the sphere, going all the way around it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The circular field pattern around a current-carrying wire is drawn in the same lessons and looks like an obvious 'field around a round object'. A sphere also invites circular drawing.
misconceptions.correction: The force on a charge near a sphere points straight out from the centre or straight in towards it, never sideways, so the lines must be straight and radial. Draw the sphere, then draw lines outwards from it like spokes on a wheel.

misconceptions.question: Which way do the arrows point on the field lines around a positively charged sphere?
misconceptions.correct: Away from the sphere. On a negatively charged sphere the arrows point towards it.
misconceptions.misconception: The arrows always point towards the charged object, because a field pulls things in.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Fields are introduced through attraction and through gravity, where everything is pulled inwards, so 'field means pull towards' becomes the default.
misconceptions.correction: The arrow shows the direction of the force on a positive charge placed at that point. A positive sphere would push it away, so arrows point outwards; a negative sphere would pull it in, so arrows point inwards.

misconceptions.question: Is there any field in the gaps between the field lines?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The field fills the whole space around the charged object. The lines are just a way of drawing it.
misconceptions.misconception: The field only exists along the lines, so a charge in a gap between two lines would feel nothing.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Diagrams show a small number of lines, and students take the drawing literally instead of as a sample of a continuous field.
misconceptions.correction: You could draw as many lines as you like; where they go is your choice, and the field is unchanged. The spacing carries the meaning - lines close together mean a strong field - not the presence or absence of ink at one point.

misconceptions.question: Where is the electric field around a charged object strongest?
misconceptions.correct: Close to the charged object. The further away from the charged object, the weaker the field.
misconceptions.misconception: The field builds up as it spreads out, so it is stronger further away, or it stops altogether at the end of the drawn lines.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Field diagrams are drawn to a fixed size, so the last line looks like an edge. Students also picture the field spreading like a beam that widens and so covers more.
misconceptions.correction: Move a charged object slowly towards a charged sphere: the force on it grows as it gets closer. Field lines are drawn closest together at the surface for exactly that reason, and they are not drawn to infinity only because the paper runs out.

misconceptions.question: Does the force between two charged objects depend on how far apart they are?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The force gets stronger as the distance between the objects decreases.
misconceptions.misconception: The force depends only on the charge on the objects, so moving them closer does not change it - they either affect each other or they do not.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The rule 'like repels, unlike attracts' is learned as a yes-or-no rule, so the force is treated as switched on rather than as something with a size that varies.
misconceptions.correction: The field is strongest close to a charged object, so a second charged object placed there experiences a bigger force. Closer means a stronger field, which means a stronger force.

misconceptions.question: What actually moves when a spark jumps across a gap?
misconceptions.correct: Electrons move across the gap through the air, once the field is strong enough for the air to conduct.
misconceptions.misconception: The positive charge jumps across the gap, and this can only happen at the moment the two objects touch.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Positive charge is drawn as a moving quantity in circuit work, and the shock is usually felt just as a hand reaches a door handle, so contact and spark seem to be the same event.
misconceptions.correction: Only electrons are free to move. They cross the gap before contact is made, which is why a spark can be seen jumping to a finger that has not yet arrived, and why the crack is heard a moment before touching.

misconceptions.question: Air is an insulator, so how can charge cross a gap of air in a spark?
misconceptions.correct: A strong enough electric field pulls electrons off atoms in the air. The air then contains charged particles that are free to move, so it conducts and charge crosses the gap.
misconceptions.misconception: Air can never conduct, so a spark must be something else - a flash of light on the surface, or heat from friction.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Air is taught as an insulator with no conditions attached, so a conducting path through it looks impossible and the spark gets explained away.
misconceptions.correction: Air insulates only while its atoms are neutral. A strong field ionises them, and ionised air conducts. This is why the spark appears suddenly, once enough charge has built up to make the field strong enough.

misconceptions.question: Does charge spread out over an insulator after it has been rubbed?
misconceptions.correct: No. Charge cannot flow through an insulating material, so it stays on the part of the surface that was rubbed.
misconceptions.misconception: Charge always spreads itself out evenly over the whole object, wherever it was put on.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Charge is pictured as a fluid, and current work teaches that charge flows readily. Nothing in the demonstration shows the student where on the rod the charge is sitting.
misconceptions.correction: Only conductors let charge move through them. Rub one end of a polythene rod and only that end attracts a suspended rod; the other end does almost nothing. That is the difference between static charge on an insulator and current in a conductor.

mcqs.stem: Two insulating materials are rubbed against each other. Which statement describes what happens?

options.text: Electrons are rubbed off one material and on to the other material.
options.rationale: This is what the specification states: negatively charged electrons are rubbed off one material and on to the other, leaving one negatively charged and one positively charged.

options.text: Rubbing creates new charge on the surfaces of both of the materials.
options.rationale: Students who learned friction as a way of producing heat treat 'producing static electricity' the same way, as making something new rather than moving it.

options.text: Protons are rubbed off one material and on to the other material.
options.rationale: A student who knows a positive charge appears assumes positive particles must have travelled to produce it.

options.text: Electrons are rubbed off both materials and lost into the air nearby.
options.rationale: Picked by students who accept that electrons move but have no destination in mind for them, so the charge is imagined to escape rather than transfer.

mcqs.stem: A polythene rod is rubbed with a dry cloth. The rod becomes negatively charged. What is the charge on the cloth?

options.text: A smaller positive charge, because the cloth keeps most of its electrons.
options.rationale: Confuses how many electrons are left behind with how much charge was transferred, so the two charges are imagined to be unequal.

options.text: An equal positive charge, because the cloth lost electrons to the rod.
options.rationale: The material that gains electrons becomes negatively charged and the material that loses them is left with an equal positive charge.

options.text: An equal positive charge, because protons moved from the rod to the cloth.
options.rationale: Reaches the right charge by the wrong route; a student who thinks positive charge is carried on to an object will accept this reasoning.

options.text: No charge at all, because the charge was created on the rod by rubbing.
options.rationale: If rubbing is thought to make charge, only the object being rubbed needs to end up charged and the cloth is forgotten.

mcqs.stem: Why is the positive charge left on one rubbed material equal in size to the negative charge on the other?

options.text: Because rubbing makes equal amounts of new positive and negative charge.
options.rationale: Keeps the equality but explains it by creation of charge, which is how students who think rubbing generates charge account for the pairing.

options.text: Because charge made by rubbing spreads out evenly between the materials.
options.rationale: Sharing sounds like a reason for equal amounts, and it avoids having to think about individual electrons.

options.text: Because every electron gained by one material is one lost by the other.
options.rationale: The charges are equal because they arise from the same transfer: the surplus of electrons on one material exactly matches the shortfall on the other.

options.text: Because equal numbers of protons and electrons move in opposite directions.
options.rationale: A symmetrical two-way transfer looks like the neatest way to produce two equal and opposite charges.

mcqs.stem: A student rubs a metal rod held in her hand with a dry cloth. The rod shows no sign of being charged. Why not?

options.text: Metals are unable to gain or lose any electrons when they are rubbed.
options.rationale: A student who has not linked charging to insulation invents a property of metals to explain the failed demonstration.

options.text: The cloth becomes charged as well, so the two charges cancel each other.
options.rationale: The equal and opposite charges are known to be there, and cancelling is a familiar way to make an unwanted result disappear.

options.text: The charge spreads over the whole rod, so it becomes too weak to detect.
options.rationale: Charge is imagined as a fluid thinning out as it spreads, which sounds like a reason for a rod that shows nothing.

options.text: Charge flows through the metal and her body, so none stays on the rod.
options.rationale: Static charge builds up only on insulating materials. A metal conducts, so charge transferred by rubbing flows away to earth through the hand.

mcqs.stem: Two charged objects are brought close together but do not touch. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Objects with the same type of charge repel; different types attract.
options.rationale: Two objects that carry the same type of charge repel, and two objects that carry different types of charge attract.

options.text: Objects with the same type of charge attract; different types repel.
options.rationale: The rule is remembered as a pair but with the two halves swapped, which is the most common error once 'like' and 'unlike' blur.

options.text: The objects only push or pull once their surfaces are touching.
options.rationale: Chosen by students whose experience of force is entirely by contact, so a force across a gap is rejected.

options.text: The objects attract each other, whatever charges they carry.
options.rationale: Generalised from the classic demonstration of a rubbed rod picking things up, which only ever shows attraction.

mcqs.stem: Two polythene rods are each rubbed with the same cloth. One is hung on a thread and the other is brought near it. What happens, and why?

options.text: It swings towards it, because both rods carry the same type of charge.
options.rationale: Identifies the charges correctly but applies the reversed rule that like charges attract.

options.text: It swings away, because both rods carry the same type of charge.
options.rationale: Rubbing identical rods with the same cloth gives both the same type of charge, and two objects carrying the same type of charge repel.

options.text: It stays still, because the two rods are not yet touching each other.
options.rationale: Consistent with a belief that a force needs contact, so nothing should happen until the rods meet.

options.text: It swings away, because the rods carry different types of charge.
options.rationale: Right prediction, wrong reason: the student recalls that repulsion happens but pairs it with unlike charges.

mcqs.stem: Which observation is the best evidence that charged objects exert forces on one another when not in contact?

options.text: Two charged rods push each other apart when their ends are touching.
options.rationale: Shows a force between charged objects, but with contact, so it is exactly the evidence that does not settle the question.

options.text: A rubbed rod feels warm to the touch after it has been rubbed hard.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who associate rubbing with heating and treat any effect of rubbing as evidence about charge.

options.text: A suspended charged rod turns away as a second charged rod nears it.
options.rationale: The suspended rod moves while a gap remains, so a force is acting between two charged objects that are not in contact.

options.text: A magnet attracts a steel pin without the two objects ever touching.
options.rationale: It is evidence of a non-contact force, but a magnetic one; students who file charge and magnetism together see no difference.

mcqs.stem: A charged polythene rod repels another charged polythene rod. A student says this shows the rods are magnetic. Which response is correct?

options.text: Yes - repulsion across a gap can only happen between magnetic poles.
options.rationale: Magnetism is the only non-contact repulsion many students have handled, so it becomes the only available explanation.

options.text: Yes - rubbing a plastic rod turns it into a weak permanent magnet.
options.rationale: Supplies a mechanism for the magnetic idea, and rubbing is genuinely used to magnetise steel, which makes it sound reasonable.

options.text: No - but the rods must carry different types of charge to repel.
options.rationale: Rejects magnetism correctly but then applies the reversed rule, attributing repulsion to unlike charges.

options.text: No - the rods repel because both carry the same type of charge.
options.rationale: Both rods were charged the same way, so they carry the same type of charge and repel. This is an electrostatic force, not magnetism.

mcqs.stem: A student walks across a nylon carpet and gets a small shock as her hand approaches a metal door handle. Why?

options.text: Rubbing has charged the student, and charge moves across the small gap.
options.rationale: Rubbing between shoes and carpet transfers electrons, charging the student; the charge then crosses the gap to the earthed handle, which is the spark she feels.

options.text: Positive charges jump from the metal handle across the gap to her hand.
options.rationale: Students who picture positive charge as the thing that moves reverse both the carrier and the direction of the transfer.

options.text: Air cannot conduct, so the shock comes from friction heating her skin.
options.rationale: Air is remembered as an insulator with no exceptions, so a different cause has to be found for the shock.

options.text: Walking creates new charge, which the metal handle then destroys again.
options.rationale: Fits a picture in which charge is made by rubbing and used up on contact rather than transferred between objects.

mcqs.stem: Charge builds up on an object until a spark suddenly jumps to a nearby earthed metal object. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: Air always insulates, so the charge must travel along a damp surface.
options.rationale: Keeps air as a perfect insulator and finds another conducting route, which sounds careful rather than wrong.

options.text: The field becomes strong enough to pull electrons off atoms in the air.
options.rationale: The field in the gap grows as charge builds up; once it is strong enough it ionises the air, the air conducts, and charge crosses the gap as a spark.

options.text: Protons move across the gap from the object to the earthed metal.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who believe positive particles carry charge from place to place; protons are in fact fixed in nuclei.

options.text: The field is weakest at the surface, so charge escapes from there first.
options.rationale: Uses the reversed rule about field strength and distance, and 'escaping where it is weakest' sounds like an explanation.

mcqs.stem: Two acetate rods are each rubbed with a dry cloth. Both become positively charged. Which explanation in terms of electrons is correct?

options.text: Each rod gained protons from its cloth, so the two rods now repel.
options.rationale: Right about the repulsion, wrong about the particle; students explain a positive charge by something positive arriving.

options.text: Rubbing made new positive charge on each rod, which the cloths took.
options.rationale: Charge is treated as manufactured by rubbing, so the cloth is given a role in removing it rather than in supplying electrons.

options.text: Each rod lost electrons to its cloth, so the two rods now repel.
options.rationale: Losing electrons leaves each rod positively charged, and two objects carrying the same type of charge repel each other.

options.text: Each rod lost electrons to its cloth, so the two rods now attract.
options.rationale: The electron transfer is understood, but the force rule is reversed so like charges are expected to pull together.

options.text: The path a charged object follows when it is released near a charge.
options.rationale: Arrowed lines look like journeys, especially to students who have just drawn ray diagrams.

options.text: The lines on the surface of a charged object along which charge sits.
options.rationale: Takes the drawing literally and places the field on the object rather than in the space around it.

options.text: The stream of electrons that flows away from a charged object.
options.rationale: Confuses a field with a current; students who know electrons carry charge expect something to be moving.

options.text: The region round a charged object where another charge feels a force.
options.rationale: A charged object creates an electric field around itself, and a second charged object placed in that field experiences a force.

mcqs.stem: How does the strength of the electric field around a charged sphere change with distance from the sphere?

options.text: It is strongest close to the sphere and gets weaker further away.
options.rationale: The electric field is strongest close to the charged object, and the further away from it, the weaker the field.

options.text: It is weakest close to the sphere and gets stronger further away.
options.rationale: Students who picture the field spreading and widening think of it as gathering strength as it goes.

options.text: It has the same strength everywhere until the field lines end.
options.rationale: Reads the diagram as a fixed object with an edge, so strength is uniform inside it and zero outside.

options.text: It is strongest at a fixed distance out from the sphere's surface.
options.rationale: Invented from diagrams where lines look most crowded a little way out; it sounds precise and so feels expert.

mcqs.stem: A charged sphere is moved closer to a second charged object. What happens to the force on the second object?

options.text: It gets weaker, because the field is stronger further from the sphere.
options.rationale: Follows consistently from the reversed rule that a field grows stronger with distance.

options.text: It gets stronger, because the field is stronger nearer the sphere.
options.rationale: The field is strongest close to the charged object, so the force on a second charged object gets stronger as the distance decreases.

options.text: It stays the same, because the charge on the sphere has not changed.
options.rationale: Treats the force as depending only on the charges, so distance is seen as irrelevant to its size.

options.text: It stays at zero, because the two objects are still not touching.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who require contact before any force can act at all.

mcqs.stem: Which description matches the electric field pattern that should be drawn for an isolated positively charged sphere?

options.text: Circles drawn all the way round the sphere, with arrows going clockwise.
options.rationale: Borrowed from the circular magnetic field pattern around a current-carrying wire, drawn in the same part of the course.

options.text: Parallel lines spaced evenly across the sphere, with arrows pointing up.
options.rationale: A uniform field is the other pattern students have seen drawn, and evenly spaced parallel lines look tidy and deliberate.

options.text: Straight lines spreading out all round the sphere, with arrows pointing out.
options.rationale: The field of an isolated charged sphere is radial. The arrows point away from a positively charged sphere, and the lines are closest together at the surface.

options.text: Straight lines spreading out all round the sphere, with arrows pointing in.
options.rationale: The shape is right but the direction is reversed, by students who assume a field always pulls objects inwards.

mcqs.stem: In the field diagram for a charged sphere, why are the field lines drawn closer together near the surface?

options.text: Because charge can only be found where the lines have been drawn in.
options.rationale: Reads the lines as real objects marking where charge sits, rather than as a representation of the field.

options.text: Because a charged object placed there would travel along those lines.
options.rationale: Treats field lines as tracks, so crowding is explained as more routes rather than as a stronger field.

options.text: Because the lines must meet at the surface, where the field ends.
options.rationale: Gives the field a boundary at the sphere, which fits a picture in which the field starts weak and builds up outwards.

options.text: Because the field is stronger there than it is further from the sphere.
options.rationale: Spacing shows field strength: the lines are closest where the field is strongest, which is close to the charged object.

mcqs.stem: A student says there is no field in the gaps between the field lines on a diagram. Which response is correct?

options.text: Wrong - the field fills the space, and the lines are a way of showing it.
options.rationale: The number of lines drawn is a choice; the field exists throughout the region around the charged object, and the spacing of the lines shows its strength.

options.text: Right - the field only exists along the lines that have been drawn on.
options.rationale: Takes the diagram literally, which is exactly the reasoning behind the student's claim.

options.text: Right - the lines show the only paths that a charge is able to follow.
options.rationale: Supports the claim with the track model of field lines, which makes the gaps look like empty ground.

options.text: Wrong - but the field is only found beyond the last line on the page.
options.rationale: Rejects the claim yet still gives the field an edge, placing it where the diagram happens to stop.

mcqs.stem: How does the idea of an electric field explain the force between two charged objects that are not touching?

options.text: The two fields must meet and touch before either object feels a force.
options.rationale: Keeps the requirement for contact but moves it from the objects to their fields, which feels like a compromise.

options.text: Each object sits in the other's field, so each one experiences a force.
options.rationale: A charged object creates a field around itself, and a second charged object placed in that field experiences a force, so no contact is needed.

options.text: Each field reaches out a fixed distance, and beyond that there is none.
options.rationale: Gives the field a sharp edge, a picture drawn straight from diagrams in which the lines stop.

options.text: One object pushes on the air, and the air then pushes the other object.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who need a material go-between before they will accept a force acting across a gap.
